**On Having a Thousand Words**

There's something strange about being handed a number like this — a thousand words, as if that were a unit of thought rather than a unit of typing. A thousand words is not a thought. A thought can happen in three words or in ten thousand and still be the same size in the mind. But here we are, and the constraint is oddly clarifying, the way a deadline makes you discover you actually have an opinion about something you thought you didn't.

I want to write about whatever comes to me, which is the hardest instruction in the world disguised as the easiest. "Whatever comes to you" assumes that something is waiting just behind a door, fully formed, and all I have to do is open it. In practice it's more like standing in a dark room and feeling along the walls for a light switch that may not exist. You find things by touch you didn't know were there. A coat. A shelf. A draft of cold air from somewhere unaccounted for.

So let me feel along the wall.

The first thing my hand finds is the idea of limits. A thousand words is a kind of room — small enough that you can hear yourself in it, large enough to turn around. Most of what people write is either too cramped to breathe in or so sprawling that nothing in it has weight, because weight requires walls to push against. I think this is true of more than writing. A life with no constraints isn't free; it's diffuse. You need the wall to know you're moving.

I think about how children understand this instinctively, before anyone teaches them otherwise. Give a child unlimited time and unlimited materials and ask them to make something, and they will often freeze or wander, picking up one object and dropping it for another, never settling. But give them ten minutes and three colors and they'll make something with a kind of ferocious, total commitment, because the boundary has done half the work of deciding for them. The boundary isn't the enemy of the work. It's the thing that makes the work possible at all, the riverbank without which the water just becomes a swamp.

This is, I suspect, why people who say "I could write a novel, I just need the time" rarely write the novel even when given the time, while people locked in genuinely terrible circumstances — prison, illness, war — have produced some of the most enduring books in human history. Not because suffering is good for art, which is a lie we should stop telling ourselves, but because constraint focuses. The hand that has nothing else to hold onto holds the pen tighter.

My hand moves along the wall further and finds something else: the strange comfort of being told what to do. "Write whatever comes to you" sounds like freedom but functions like permission. There is a difference between those two things that we don't talk about enough. Freedom is the absence of walls. Permission is someone telling you it's all right to walk into the room you were already standing outside of, afraid. Most of us are not short on freedom. We are short on permission — the small, specific kind that says: yes, this thought you're having, the one that seems too slight or too strange to bother writing down, that one's allowed. Go ahead.

I think about how much human creativity is gated not by ability but by this exact, tiny psychological toll booth. The number of good sentences that die in someone's head because they decided, in a fraction of a second, that the sentence wasn't worth the trouble of typing — that toll booth charges more than we admit. A prompt like this one, vague and total, is in a way a gift: it removes the toll. There is no wrong answer to "whatever comes to you," so for once, nothing is being judged against a target it might miss.

And yet even now, writing this, I notice myself doing the thing humans do, which is building the wall back even after being told there isn't one. I am still organizing. I am still making sure this has a shape, a little arc, something that feels like it's going somewhere rather than just be a thousand words of static. Maybe that's not obedience to a rule but something more basic: we cannot help but make shapes. Even free association tends, after a while, to start rhyming with itself. Say enough true things in a row and a structure appears whether or not you went looking for one, the way constellations appear in stars that have no actual relation to one another except the accident of our looking up at the right angle.

So maybe that's what's actually "come to me" — not a single idea but the demonstration of something about how ideas work at all: that they need a little resistance to become visible, the way you can't see your own breath except in cold air. A formless prompt forces the mind to supply its own form, and watching it do that, almost against its will, is more interesting than anything I could have decided in advance to say.

I'm near the end of the room now, the thousand words closing in like a tide that was never dramatic, just steady. There's no grand conclusion waiting at the back wall, no profound thing I was secretly building toward. That's all right. Not everything needs to resolve. Sometimes the only honest ending is the one where you notice the room is the size it is, that you've reached the place where the wall actually is, and that this too was worth doing — not because it proves anything, but because for a few hundred words you weren't standing outside the door deciding whether to walk in.

You were already inside, feeling along the wall, finding the switch, or not finding it, and writing anyway in the dark.
